news_title: Oysters from Virginia river continue to test positive for Salmonella - Food Safety News
efet_title: Oysters from Virginia river continue to test positive for Salmonella - Food Safety News
efet_body:
The Virginia Department of Health is reporting that a third round of oysters taken from Little Wicomico Oyster Company cages on Nov. 2 tested positive for Salmonella, representing three of eight meat samples from two of the company’s four leases.
The Little Wicomico River in Northumberland County, VA, remains closed to shellfish harvest with no end date. CDC counts 28 people sick with Salmonella Telelkebir in 13 states, five of them hospitalized and none dead. Recalled oysters were harvested Sept. 18 through Oct. 8 and shipped to 16 states and the District of Columbia.
On Oct. 13, 400 oysters were pulled from the company’s cages and processed into eight meat samples; all eight were positive, carrying Salmonella Telelkebir, Newport, Hartford and Braenderup. On Oct. 21 a second 400-oyster round was positive on three of the four leases, with Telelkebir, Newport, Hartford and Thompson. On Nov. 2 a third round was positive on three of eight samples from two of four leases. A fourth round was collected Nov. 9 and results are pending at the state lab.
The river cannot reopen until three rounds in a row come back clean.
Virginia also looked for where the Salmonella might be coming from. Forty-seven water samples collected Oct. 22 were tested for HF183, a marker of human sewage, and for Enterococci, a general fecal indicator. HF183 was negative in all 47 and Enterococci ran from below the detection limit to 120 MPN per 100 milliliters. The state health department says the data do not point to a significant sewage release.
Eight bird-feces samples collected Nov. 2 were negative for Salmonella. Oysters from the river’s public harvest grounds, sampled Oct. 26, were negative. Water and oysters from the public grounds collected Nov. 4 went to the University of North Carolina and are pending.
The health department closed the river by emergency order on Oct. 9. When that 30-day order ran out, it replaced it with
Shellfish Area Condemnation 010-105
, with no expiration date.
Eleven of the 28 outbreak patients reported eating raw oysters, and tag and traceback records for seven of them led back to the Little Wicomico River. Two of those seven ate oysters from this river only.
FDA’s safety alert
, lists distribution to California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and the District of Columbia, and says the oysters may have been shipped further.
The recall covers shellstock oysters harvested from the Little Wicomico River between Sept. 18 and Oct. 8, tagged Little Wicomico River, VA, or Little Wicomico River Lower, VA. Publix sold some of them as James River Oysters through Oct. 14. If you shucked and froze oyster meat in late September or early October and are not sure where it came from, throw it out.

news_title: Everything Sprouts E. coli and Salmonella Outbreak Ends - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Everything Sprouts E. coli and Salmonella Outbreak Ends - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
The Everything Sprouts E. coli and Salmonella outbreak has ended with 77 people sick in 16 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (
CDC
). That is an increase of one more patient since the
last update
was issued on October 1, 2026; the new patent lives in Minnesota. There were three strains of E. coli in this outbreak: E. coli O26:H11, O103:H25, and O168:H8. The strain of Salmonella was Salmonella Agona. The company is located in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
The case count by state is: Florida (2), Iowa (2), Indiana (1), Kansas (1), Michigan (1), Minnesota (29), North Carolina (3), North Dakota (3), New Hampshire (1), New York (2), Oregon (1), Pennsylvania (1), South Carolina (1), South Dakota (1), Washington (1), and Wisconsin (27). Illness onset dates range from May 31, 2026 to October 19, 2026. The patient age range is from 12 to 94 years. Six people were hospitalized. Sixty-four people were sick with E. coli, 10 were sick with Salmonella, and three patients were sick with both Salmonella and E. coli.
Several recalls were issued in relation to this outbreak. The company’s
Robust Radish
mix was recalled, as was their alfalfa sprouts which were used in the company’s
Crunchy Protein and Zesty Garlic
sprout mixes.
Everything and Calco alfalfa sprouts
were recalled in August 2026. And International Sprout Holding
recalled
their alfalfa sprout seeds in September 2026.
Of the 52 people interviewed by public health officials, 41, or 79%, said they ate sprouts before they got sick, and 36 of those patients specifically recalled eating alfalfa sprouts. This percentage was significantly higher than the 8.7% of respondents who reported eating any sprouts during the same time frame. That suggests people in this outbreak got sick from eating alfalfa sprouts.
Some illness clusters were identified in this outbreak. Seven were identified in Minnesota and Wisconsin. The most commonly reported food item was alfalfa sprouts.
Whole genome sequencing performed on patient samples showed that their samples were closely related genetically. This suggests that people in this outbreak got sick from eating the same food. Finally, traceback information from Minnesota and Wisconsin restaurants identified Everything Sprouts were a source of illness. The FDA traced illnesses to a single lot of alfalfa seeds from a common supplier.

news_title: UK Salmonella outbreak captures public’s attention
efet_title: UK Salmonella outbreak captures public’s attention
efet_body:
Foodborne outbreaks climbed to the top of people’s minds in September, according to a survey covering most of the United Kingdom.
Findings come from the Consumer Insights Tracker, an online monthly survey commissioned by the Food Standards Agency (FSA). It monitors the behavior and attitudes of 2,000 people aged 16 and older in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
In September 2026, food poisoning outbreaks became the most commonly recalled food safety topic, with 45 percent of respondents saying they had seen, heard or read something about this subject in the past month, a large rise from 19 percent in August and 15 percent in July.

news_title: Baby goat found to be cause of E. coli outbreak
efet_title: Baby goat found to be cause of E. coli outbreak
efet_body:
A baby goat at a petting zoo at a pumpkin patch attraction has been found to be the likely source of an E. coli outbreak.
The animal at Bengston’s Pumpkin Farm was identified by the Will County Health Department. The department has reported that DNA testing found the goat to be infected with the same strain of E. coli that infected people who visited the farm.
Officials from the health department said they worked with the farm and a veterinarian to collect samples from animals in the petting zoo and other areas throughout the property in Homer Glen.
Several animals tested positive for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, but additional testing identified one baby goat whose bacteria were closely related to those found in confirmed human cases.
“These test results provide an important link in our investigation,” said Sean Conners, Director of Environmental Health at the Will County Health Department.
“While E. coli bacteria are commonly found in animals, our testing identified a close genetic match between bacteria from confirmed human cases and a baby goat at the petting zoo. We also thoroughly reviewed food service operations at the farm and did not identify any concerns.”
The health department also confirmed two additional cases after reviewing the lab results. So far, seven confirmed patients have been identified. The department has not reported whether any of the patients have required hospitalization.
Investigators confirmed that signs were posted at the petting zoo entrance and exit reminding visitors to wash their hands, avoid eating around animals and leave strollers and wagons outside. Handwashing stations were also available at the exit.
Anyone who visited Bengtson’s Pumpkin Farm on or after September 29 and experienced symptoms was asked to complete a confidential survey through the
Will County Health Department
.
About E. coli infections
Anyone who has developed symptoms of E. coli infection should seek medical attention and tell their doctor about their possible exposure to the bacteria. Specific tests are required to diagnose the infections, which can mimic other illnesses.
The symptoms of E. coli infections vary for each person but often include severe stomach cramps and diarrhea, which is often bloody. Some patients may also have a fever. Most patients recover within five to seven days. Others can develop severe or life-threatening symptoms and complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
About 5 to 10 percent of those diagnosed with E. coli infections develop a potentially life-threatening kidney failure complication, known as a hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Symptoms of HUS include fever, abdominal pain, feeling very tired, decreased frequency of urination, small unexplained bruises or bleeding, and pallor.
Many people with HUS recover within a few weeks, but some suffer permanent injuries or death. This condition can occur among people of any age but is most common in children younger than five years old because of their immature immune systems, older adults because of deteriorating immune systems, and people with compromised immune systems such as cancer patients.
People who experience HUS symptoms should immediately seek emergency medical care. People with HUS will likely be hospitalized because the condition can cause other serious and ongoing problems such as hypertension, chronic kidney disease, brain damage, and neurologic problems.

The products contain sesame, a known allergen, which is not declared on the product labels. In addition, the beef product contains Worcestershire sauce that contains anchovy (fish), a known allergen, which is not declared on the product labels.
